entries.1:1: Paul introduces himself as an apostle chosen by God's will, writing together with Timothy to the church in Corinth and to all believers throughout the region. This shows the letter comes with God's authority and is meant for ordinary Christians to read and share.
entries.1:2: Paul wishes his readers grace and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ. These are not just polite words but a real blessing, asking God to show kindness and give inner calm to the people who receive it.
entries.1:3: Paul praises God, calling him the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort. This tells the reader that God is the source of every kindness and every bit of comfort they will ever need.
entries.1:4: God comforts us in all our troubles so that we can pass that same comfort on to others who are struggling. Your own hard times can become the very thing that lets you help someone else.
entries.1:5: Just as we share in Christ's sufferings, we also share richly in the comfort that comes through him. Suffering and comfort go together for a believer, and the comfort is always greater because it comes from Christ.
entries.1:6: Paul says his troubles and his comfort both work for the readers' benefit, helping them be saved and strengthened to endure the same kinds of hardship. Even a leader's suffering can be used by God to help ordinary believers.
entries.1:7: Paul is confident that just as the Corinthians share in the troubles, they will also share in the comfort. You can count on God to comfort you in proportion to what you endure.
entries.1:8: Paul wants them to know how severely they were crushed in Asia, beyond their strength, so that they even despaired of living. He is honest about how bad it got, which lets readers know that even strong believers can reach the end of themselves.
entries.1:9: They felt they had received a death sentence, and the purpose was to stop trusting in themselves and trust instead in God, who raises the dead. When you hit bottom, it can push you to rely on God rather than your own resources.
entries.1:10: God rescued them from a deadly danger, and they hope he will keep rescuing them. Past rescues give you reason to expect God's help in the future.
entries.1:11: The Corinthians can help by praying for Paul, so that many people's prayers will lead to many people thanking God for the answer. Your prayers for others really matter and become part of what God does.
entries.1:12: Paul's confidence is that he and his companions lived honestly and sincerely, relying on God's grace rather than human cleverness, especially toward the Corinthians. A clear conscience and straightforward conduct are worth more than worldly wisdom.
entries.1:13: Paul says he writes nothing to them other than what they can plainly read and understand, and he hopes they will keep understanding it fully. He is not hiding meanings or being tricky with them.
entries.1:14: They have already partly understood that Paul and his team are their pride and joy, just as the Corinthians are Paul's, on the day the Lord Jesus returns. Believers will be each other's joy when Christ comes back.
entries.1:15: Paul had planned to visit them first so they would get a second experience of God's grace through him. His plans were meant to bless them, not to slight them.
entries.1:16: He intended to pass through Corinth on his way to Macedonia, come back to them, and have them help him on his journey to Judea. His travel plans were practical and included them.
entries.1:17: Paul asks whether his change of plans looked like shallow flip-flopping, as if he said yes and no at the same time. He is defending himself against the charge of being unreliable.
entries.1:18: Paul calls God as witness that his message to them was not a mixture of yes and no. What he told them about God could be trusted.
entries.1:19: The message about Jesus that Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy preached among them was not yes and no but a firm yes. Jesus himself is completely reliable, not shifting or uncertain.
entries.1:20: All of God's promises find their yes in Christ, and through him we say amen to God's glory. Every promise God made is fulfilled and made certain in Jesus, so you can trust what God has said.
entries.1:21: It is God who keeps both Paul and the Corinthians firm in Christ and who has given them his grace. Your stability in faith is God's work, not your own achievement.
entries.1:22: God has set his seal on us and given us the Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee of what is coming. The Spirit inside you is God's down payment and proof that more is promised.
entries.1:23: Paul calls God as witness that he stayed away from Corinth out of concern for them, to spare them. His delay was meant to be kind, not neglectful.
entries.1:24: Paul says he does not boss them around in their faith but works with them for their joy, since it is their faith that holds them up. Leaders are meant to help believers rejoice, not to control them.
entries.2:1: Paul decided not to visit the Corinthians again because his last visit had caused them pain. It means he chose to spare them rather than bring more sadness.
entries.2:2: If Paul made them sad, the people who should cheer him up would be the very ones he had hurt. His point is that causing them pain would only hurt himself too.
entries.2:3: Paul wrote a letter instead of coming in person so he would not be hurt by the people who should bring him joy. He trusted that his happiness and theirs were tied together.
entries.2:4: Paul wrote that letter while deeply distressed and weeping, not to hurt them but to show how much he loved them. It reminds readers that hard words from a loving person can come from care, not cruelty.
entries.2:5: If someone caused trouble, the hurt was felt not just by Paul but by the whole church to some degree. He says this gently so he does not come down too hard on the person.
entries.2:6: The punishment the church gave that person was enough. It means the discipline had done its job and did not need to go further.
entries.2:7: Now the church should forgive and comfort him so he is not crushed by too much sorrow. The point is that correction should end in restoration, not despair.
entries.2:8: Paul asks the church to show their love for this person in concrete actions. It means real love has to be demonstrated, not just felt.
entries.2:9: Paul wrote earlier to test whether they would follow his instructions in everything. It shows he was checking their willingness to obey, not just their words.
entries.2:10: When the church forgives someone, Paul forgives too, and he does it on behalf of Christ and for their sake. It means forgiveness is done together, in Christ's presence.
entries.2:11: Paul warns that unforgiveness gives Satan an opening to harm the church. It means we should forgive because we know how the enemy works and do not want to be outsmarted by him.
entries.2:12: When Paul arrived in Troas to preach the good news, he found a real opportunity for the work there. It means God opens doors for the gospel, even when other things are unsettled.
entries.2:13: Paul was still restless because his coworker Titus had not arrived, so he left Troas and went on to Macedonia. It shows that even a good opportunity can be set aside when personal concern weighs on someone.
entries.2:14: Paul praises God, who always leads us to victory in Christ and spreads the knowledge of him everywhere through us. It means God uses ordinary believers to make himself known.
entries.2:15: Paul says believers are like a pleasing fragrance of Christ to God, both among those being saved and those who are perishing. It means our lives carry the scent of Christ to everyone around us.
entries.2:16: The same message smells like death to some and life to others, depending on how they respond. Paul asks who is adequate for such a serious task, showing humility about the calling.
entries.2:17: Paul says he and his companions do not peddle God's word for money but speak honestly as people sent from God. It means God's message should be handled truthfully, not used for personal gain.
entries.3:1: Paul asks if he really needs to prove himself or bring letters of recommendation like some other teachers did. It means the reader doesn't need outside proof to trust a genuine ministry.
entries.3:2: The Corinthian believers themselves are Paul's letter of recommendation, written on his heart for everyone to see. It means a changed life is the best evidence that someone's work is real.
entries.3:3: The Corinthians are like a letter from Christ, written not with ink or on stone but by God's Spirit on human hearts. It means God's work in people's lives is visible and living, not just words on paper.
entries.3:4: Paul says this confidence he has comes through Christ and is directed toward God. It means our assurance doesn't rest on ourselves but on what Christ has done.
entries.3:5: Paul insists he can't claim any credit for what he does; his ability comes from God. It means we shouldn't boast about our own strength, because anything good we do is enabled by God.
entries.3:6: God made Paul able to serve a new agreement based on the Spirit, not on written rules, because rules alone bring death while the Spirit gives life. It means the Christian life is powered by God's Spirit, not just by trying to keep rules.
entries.3:7: The old law carved in stone came with real glory, so bright that Moses had to cover his face. It means even something temporary and glorious shows how much greater God's new way must be.
entries.3:8: If the old way had glory, the work of the Spirit will have far greater glory. It means we should expect the Spirit's work to outshine anything that came before.
entries.3:9: The old law brought condemnation, yet it had glory; the Spirit brings righteousness, so its glory is much greater. It means the good news of being made right with God is far more glorious than the law that exposed our guilt.
entries.3:10: The earlier glory almost seems like no glory at all next to the greater glory that replaces it. It means the new thing God does is so much better that the old fades by comparison.
entries.3:11: If something temporary had glory, something that lasts forever will have much more. It means the lasting covenant we have in Christ is far more glorious than anything that was only for a time.
entries.3:12: Because we have this hope, Paul and his companions speak openly and boldly. It means confidence in God's promises should make us honest and unashamed in sharing them.
entries.3:13: Paul doesn't hide behind a veil like Moses did to keep Israel from seeing the end of the old order. It means we don't need to conceal the truth; we can be open about what God is doing.
entries.3:14: Their minds were hardened, and even now when the old agreement is read, that same veil remains unless it is removed in Christ. It means people can miss the point of Scripture until they come to Jesus.
entries.3:15: Even today, when the law of Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts. It means reading the Bible without Christ can leave a person blind to its real meaning.
entries.3:16: When a person turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. It means coming to Jesus opens our eyes to understand God's word.
entries.3:17: The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. It means God's Spirit sets people free rather than keeping them in bondage.
entries.3:18: With unveiled faces we reflect the Lord's glory and are being changed into his likeness more and more by the Spirit. It means as we look to God, he gradually makes us more like Christ.
entries.4:1: Paul says that because God mercifully gave him and his coworkers this new work to do, they don't lose heart or give up. For the reader, it means any service God gives you is a gift of mercy, so you can keep going without quitting.
entries.4:2: Paul refuses to use hidden, shameful methods or to twist God's word to trick people; instead he tells the plain truth and lets God and people's consciences judge him. For the reader, it means honesty and openness should mark how you speak and act, especially about God.
entries.4:3: If some people can't see the good news, Paul says it's hidden only from those who are headed for ruin. For the reader, it's a sober warning that rejecting the message leaves a person in the dark.
entries.4:4: Paul says the god of this world, meaning Satan, has blinded the minds of those who don't believe, so the light of the good news about Christ doesn't reach them. For the reader, it explains why some people just can't see the truth, and it should move you to pray for them.
entries.4:5: Paul says his preaching isn't about promoting himself but about Jesus Christ as Lord, with Paul himself serving the people for Jesus' sake. For the reader, it means the message should point to Jesus, not to the messenger.
entries.4:6: Paul says the same God who created light out of darkness has shined light into believers' hearts, giving them knowledge of God's glory seen in Jesus. For the reader, it means your coming to know God is God's own work of light in your heart.
entries.4:7: Paul says this great treasure of knowing God is carried in ordinary, fragile people like clay jars, so it's clear the power comes from God and not from us. For the reader, it means your weakness doesn't disqualify you; it lets God's power show.
entries.4:8: Paul describes being pressed hard on every side but not crushed, and being puzzled but not left without a way forward. For the reader, it means hard times are real, but they don't have to trap or defeat you.
entries.4:9: Paul says they are hunted and knocked down but never abandoned or destroyed. For the reader, it means even when life hits hard, God has not left you on your own.
entries.4:10: Paul says his body constantly carries the dying of Jesus, so that Jesus' life can also be seen in him. For the reader, it means when you share in suffering for Jesus, his life becomes visible through you.
entries.4:11: Paul says that while they are still alive they face death constantly for Jesus' sake, so that Jesus' life can be seen in their mortal bodies. For the reader, it means faithfulness to Jesus may cost a lot, but his life shines through it.
entries.4:12: Paul says death is at work in him and his coworkers, but life is at work in the people they serve. For the reader, it means their sacrifice brought you spiritual life, so value those who pour themselves out for others.
entries.4:13: Paul says they have the same spirit of faith as the Scripture that says a person speaks out of what they believe in their heart, so their words come from their faith. For the reader, it means what you truly believe will show up in what you say.
entries.4:14: Paul is confident that the God who raised Jesus from the dead will also raise them and bring them into his presence with the Corinthians. For the reader, it means the resurrection is your sure hope, and God will not leave you behind.
entries.4:15: Paul says they endure everything for the sake of the people they serve, so that as more people receive God's grace, more thanks and glory go to God. For the reader, it means grace received should turn into gratitude and praise.
entries.4:16: Paul says they don't wear out or quit, because even though their bodies are wearing down, their inner selves are being renewed every day. For the reader, it means aging or hardship on the outside doesn't stop God from refreshing you inside.
entries.4:17: Paul says today's troubles are light and short compared to the far greater and lasting glory they are producing for us. For the reader, it means your present pain is not the end of the story and is worth far less than what's coming.
entries.4:18: Paul says to fix your eyes not on what you can see but on what you can't see, because visible things are temporary while invisible things last forever. For the reader, it means let eternal realities, not just what's in front of you, shape your focus.
entries.5:1: Our physical body is like a temporary tent that wears out and dies, but God has prepared a permanent, eternal home for us in heaven. This means death is not the end for the believer; we have something better waiting.
entries.5:2: While we live in these weak bodies, we groan with longing to put on our heavenly, resurrected body. The reader can take comfort that longing for something better is normal and points to real hope.
entries.5:3: Paul wants to be clothed with the new body so that his spirit will not be found bare or exposed. It means the believer's hope is to be fully covered by God's resurrection life, not left naked in death.
entries.5:4: We groan under the burden of this life, not because we want to escape our bodies, but because we want our new, immortal bodies so that life can swallow up death. The reader should see that the Christian hope is resurrection, not simply escaping the body.
entries.5:5: God himself prepared us for this future and gave us his Spirit as a down payment guaranteeing what is coming. The reader can trust that the Spirit inside them is God's pledge that this hope is real.
entries.5:6: So we are always confident, even though while we live in this body we are away from the Lord's visible presence. The reader can live with courage, knowing that being physically separated from the Lord now is temporary.
entries.5:7: We live by trusting God rather than by seeing him with our eyes. The reader is reminded that faith, not sight, is how we walk through life now.
entries.5:8: We are confident and would rather leave this body and be at home with the Lord. The reader can face death with hope, knowing that being with the Lord is better.
entries.5:9: Our goal, whether at home in the body or away from it, is to please the Lord. The reader should make pleasing God their aim in every situation of life.
entries.5:10: Every one of us must stand before Christ and be judged, receiving what is due for what we did in the body, whether good or bad. The reader should live with accountability, knowing their actions matter to God.
entries.5:11: Knowing the Lord is to be feared, we try to persuade people, and God sees our hearts clearly. The reader can be honest, because God knows our true motives even when others don't.
entries.5:12: Paul isn't asking for their approval again but giving them a reason to be proud of him, so they can answer those who boast about outward appearance rather than what's in the heart. The reader should value heart-felt sincerity over show.
entries.5:13: If Paul seems crazy, it's for God's sake; if he is serious, it's for the church's benefit. The reader can see that his motives are not self-serving but aimed at God and others.
entries.5:14: Christ's love compels us, because we believe that one person died for all, meaning all were included in his death. The reader should feel the pull of that love as the reason to live for him.
entries.5:15: Christ died for all so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them. The reader is called to stop living self-centeredly and live for Christ.
entries.5:16: From now on we don't evaluate people by outward, worldly standards, even if we once knew Christ that way. The reader should see people through a new, spiritual lens rather than by appearance or status.
entries.5:17: Anyone in Christ is a new creation, with the old gone. It is not just forgiveness; it is a fresh start.
entries.5:18: All this comes from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. The reader is entrusted with the same work of helping others find peace with God.
entries.5:19: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting people's sins against them, and he gave us this message to proclaim. The reader has good news to share: God offers forgiveness rather than holding sins against us.
entries.5:20: We act as Christ's ambassadors, as though God were appealing through us, urging people to be reconciled to God. The reader represents Christ to others and should urge them toward peace with God.
entries.5:21: God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, so that in him we might become God's righteousness. The reader can receive a right standing with God as a gift, because Christ took our sin in our place.
entries.6:1: Paul says he and his coworkers are working alongside God, and he begs the Corinthians not to waste the kindness God has shown them. For the reader, it means God's grace is meant to change how you live, not just be received and forgotten.
entries.6:2: God says he heard and helped at the right moment, and Paul says that moment is now. For the reader, this means you don't need to wait for a better time to respond to God; today is the day.
entries.6:3: Paul is careful not to do anything that would make people stumble or give critics a reason to blame his work. For the reader, it means how you act matters because it can either help or hurt how others see the message you carry.
entries.6:4: Paul shows he is God's servant by enduring hardship, need, and sorrow with steady patience. For the reader, it means real service to God often shows up in how you handle hard times, not just in good ones.
entries.6:5: Paul lists concrete sufferings: beatings, jail, riots, exhausting labor, sleepless nights, and going hungry. For the reader, it means following God can involve real cost and discomfort, and that doesn't mean something is wrong.
entries.6:6: Paul points to inner qualities: a pure heart, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, and genuine love. For the reader, it means God cares about your character and inner life, not just your outward actions.
entries.6:7: Paul speaks of telling the truth and relying on God's power, with righteousness as a weapon in both hands. For the reader, it means honesty and right living, backed by God's strength, are what you fight with in life.
entries.6:8: Paul is treated with honor and dishonor, praised and slandered, called a liar yet known to be truthful. For the reader, it means people's opinions of you will vary, and you can stay faithful even when misunderstood.
entries.6:9: Paul is overlooked yet remembered by God, near death yet still alive, punished yet not killed. For the reader, it means being unnoticed or mistreated doesn't mean God has abandoned you.
entries.6:10: Paul is sorrowful yet always glad, poor yet making many rich, having nothing yet possessing everything. For the reader, it means joy and worth don't depend on circumstances or possessions.
entries.6:11: Paul tells the Corinthians he has spoken openly to them and his heart is wide open toward them. For the reader, it means honest, warm love should mark how you relate to others.
entries.6:12: Paul says the problem isn't his affection for them but their restricted affection toward him. For the reader, it means sometimes the distance in a relationship is on the other side, and honesty about that is fair.
entries.6:13: Paul asks them, as a father would ask his children, to open their hearts to him in return. For the reader, it means love given should be met with love returned, especially within a spiritual family.
entries.6:14: Paul warns against being closely tied to people who reject the faith, since right and wrong, light and dark, don't mix. For the reader, it means be careful about close partnerships that pull you away from what you believe.
entries.6:15: Paul asks what Christ and the devil, or a believer and an unbeliever, have in common. For the reader, it means some close bonds are simply incompatible with your faith and will create conflict.
entries.6:16: Paul says God's people are God's own house, and idols have no place there, since God promises to live among them. For the reader, it means your life belongs to God, and he wants to be present in it, not pushed aside.
entries.6:17: God calls his people to come out from among those who don't honor him and to stay away from what is unclean, and he will receive them. For the reader, it means following God may require leaving behind some influences and habits.
entries.6:18: God promises to be a Father to his people and to call them his sons and daughters. For the reader, it means you belong to God as family, and that relationship is his own promise, not something you earn.
entries.7:1: Since God has made us these great promises, we should clean up our lives from everything that corrupts body and spirit. Being holy is not about being perfect but about taking God seriously and letting him shape how we live.
entries.7:2: Paul asks the Corinthians to open their hearts to him and his coworkers, insisting they have never cheated, hurt, or taken advantage of anyone. He wants them to trust that his motives toward them are honest and good.
entries.7:3: Paul is not saying this to make them feel guilty or condemned. He is reminding them that they are so close to his heart that he would share life and death with them.
entries.7:4: Paul speaks to them with complete confidence and is proud of them. Even in all his troubles, they bring him great comfort and joy.
entries.7:5: When Paul arrived in Macedonia, he had no rest and faced trouble on every side, with conflicts outside and fears inside. Even strong believers go through seasons where life feels like a battle on all fronts.
entries.7:6: God, who comforts those who feel low and discouraged, comforted Paul by sending Titus. God often brings comfort to us through the arrival of a caring friend.
entries.7:7: Titus brought more than his presence; he brought news of how much the Corinthians longed for Paul, grieved over the situation, and cared for him. That report made Paul even happier.
entries.7:8: Paul's earlier letter hurt the Corinthians, and he regretted causing them pain for a while. But now he does not regret it, because the pain only lasted a short time and did its work.
entries.7:9: Paul is glad now, not because they were hurt, but because their pain led them to change their hearts and turn back to God. Their sorrow was the kind that brings good rather than loss.
entries.7:10: Sorrow that comes from God leads people to turn from sin and be saved, and no one needs to regret that. But sorrow that is only about the world's way of things leads to death.
entries.7:11: Look at what that God-focused sorrow produced in you: you cleared yourselves, got angry at the sin, felt alarm, longed to do right, and took the matter seriously. In every way you showed you were innocent in this situation.
entries.7:12: Paul did not write his letter just to address the person who did wrong or the person who was hurt. He wrote so that their genuine care for him and for the church would be clear before God.
entries.7:13: This news comforted Paul and his companions, and they were even happier to see how much joy Titus received from the Corinthians. When one part of the church is refreshed, everyone is refreshed.
entries.7:14: Paul had bragged to Titus about the Corinthians, and he was not embarrassed by how they turned out. Just as everything Paul told them was true, his good words about them to Titus also proved true.
entries.7:15: Titus's love for the Corinthians grew even stronger as he remembered how they welcomed him with respect and honored him. Treating a visiting leader with kindness leaves a lasting mark on that person's heart.
entries.7:16: Paul is filled with joy because the Corinthians have lived up to the good opinion he had of them in every way. It is a deep encouragement when people you trust in turn prove faithful.
entries.8:1: Paul tells the Corinthians good news about how God has shown kindness to the churches in Macedonia. It reminds the reader that God's generosity is real and worth noticing in other people's lives.
entries.8:2: Even though these believers were in deep trouble and very poor, they were filled with joy and gave generously to help others. It shows that hard circumstances don't have to stop us from being generous.
entries.8:3: Paul testifies that they gave as much as they could, and even beyond what they could afford, because they genuinely wanted to. It means giving is measured by the heart's willingness, not just by the amount.
entries.8:4: They urgently asked for the chance to share in the collection for needy believers. It shows that helping others in need is a privilege worth asking for, not a burden to avoid.
entries.8:5: They did far more than Paul expected: first they gave themselves to the Lord and then to Paul's team, following God's will. It means real generosity starts with giving yourself to God.
entries.8:6: Paul asked Titus, who had already begun this work, to help the Corinthians finish their collection. It means good intentions need follow-through to be completed.
entries.8:7: The Corinthians were strong in faith, speech, knowledge, earnestness, and love, and Paul wants them to be strong in generous giving too. It means generosity should be part of a well-rounded Christian life.
entries.8:8: Paul isn't commanding them but testing whether their love is genuine by comparing it with others' eagerness. It means love is shown by what we actually do, not just by what we say.
entries.8:9: Jesus was rich but became poor for our sake, so that we could become rich through him. It means our giving should mirror the self-sacrificing generosity Jesus showed us.
entries.8:10: Paul gives his advice: since they started this collection a year ago, it's to their advantage to finish it. It means finishing what you start brings real benefit.
entries.8:11: They should complete the task now, so that their willing desire matches their actual giving according to what they have. It means follow through on your good intentions with real action.
entries.8:12: If someone is willing, God accepts their gift based on what they have, not on what they lack. It means God values willingness and doesn't expect more than you can give.
entries.8:13: Paul isn't asking them to relieve others by making themselves suffer. It means giving shouldn't leave you in hardship while others are comfortable.
entries.8:14: The goal is fairness: those with plenty help those in need now, and later the reverse could happen. It means sharing keeps things balanced among God's people.
entries.8:15: Paul quotes the story of manna in the desert, where those who gathered much had nothing left over and those who gathered little had enough. It means God provides so that no one has too much or too little when people share.
entries.8:16: Paul thanks God for putting the same care for the Corinthians into Titus's heart. It means genuine concern for others is a gift from God worth being thankful for.
entries.8:17: Titus welcomed Paul's request and went to them willingly, out of his own heart. It means willing service, not forced duty, is what makes help meaningful.
entries.8:18: Paul sends along a brother who is well spoken of in all the churches for his work in sharing the good news. It means a good reputation among believers matters.
entries.8:19: The churches chose this brother to travel with Paul and help with the collection, which honors the Lord and shows their readiness. It means handling money for God's work should be done openly and with trusted people.
entries.8:20: Paul wants to avoid any criticism about how this large gift is handled. It means being careful and honest with money given for God's work protects everyone's reputation.
entries.8:21: Paul arranged things so that both the Lord and people could see the handling was honest. It means doing what is right in God's eyes and in people's eyes too.
entries.8:22: Paul sends another brother whose eagerness has been proven many times, and who is now even more eager because he trusts the Corinthians. It means proven faithfulness builds trust for bigger responsibilities.
entries.8:23: If anyone asks about Titus, he is Paul's partner working for the Corinthians; the others are representatives of the churches honoring Christ. It means these messengers deserve respect because of who they represent.
entries.8:24: Paul urges the Corinthians to show these representatives their love and prove that Paul's boasting about them was true. It means treat God's messengers well and let your love be visible in action.
entries.9:1: Paul says he doesn't really need to write to them about collecting money for fellow believers, because they already know about it. It means the reader can take encouragement that some things don't need to be explained again.
entries.9:2: Paul had bragged to the churches in Macedonia that the believers in Achaia were ready to give a year ago, and their enthusiasm stirred others to give too. It means your example can motivate other people to do good, so take that seriously.
entries.9:3: Paul is sending some brothers ahead of time so that the good things he said about the Corinthians' readiness will turn out to be true. It means he wants their follow-through to match their good intentions.
entries.9:4: Paul worries that if some Macedonians come with him and find the Corinthians unprepared, everyone involved would be embarrassed. It means it's wise to finish what you promised so no one is put to shame.
entries.9:5: Paul thought it best to send the brothers ahead to make sure the money they promised was collected beforehand, so it would look like a generous gift rather than something squeezed out of them. It means planning ahead helps your giving stay cheerful and honest.
entries.9:6: The point is simple farming logic: plant a little, harvest a little; plant generously, harvest generously. It means how you give affects what comes back, so give with an open hand.
entries.9:7: Each person should decide in their own heart what to give, not reluctantly or under pressure, because God delights in a cheerful giver. It means your giving should be your own free choice, done gladly.
entries.9:8: God is able to pour out every kind of grace on you so that you always have enough and can do every good work. It means you don't have to hoard out of fear; God supplies what you need to be generous.
entries.9:9: The psalm says a generous person scatters gifts to the poor, and their righteousness lasts forever. It means generous giving is the kind of good that God remembers and honors permanently.
entries.9:10: The same God who supplies seed to the farmer and bread to eat will supply and multiply your resources and grow the fruit of your righteousness. It means God takes care of the giver and makes their good deeds grow.
entries.9:11: You will be enriched in every way so you can be generous, and that generosity will cause people to thank God. It means your resources are a means for others to praise God, not just for your own comfort.
entries.9:12: This giving service not only meets the practical needs of fellow believers but also overflows in many thanksgivings to God. It means giving does double good: it helps people and it honors God.
entries.9:13: When people see this generous giving, they will glorify God for your obedience to the gospel and for your open-handed sharing with them and everyone. It means your giving is evidence of real faith that points people to God.
entries.9:14: Those who receive will long for you and pray for you because of the extraordinary grace of God at work in you. It means generosity creates real love and prayer between people.
entries.9:15: Paul bursts out in thanks to God for his indescribable gift, which is far beyond words. It means the greatest thing to be thankful for is God's own gift, which no language can fully express.
entries.10:1: Paul appeals to the Corinthians gently, the way Christ himself was gentle, even though some thought he was bold only in letters and timid in person. It reminds us that real strength can be humble and kind.
entries.10:2: Paul asks them to respond before he arrives so he won't have to be harsh with those who accuse him of acting from selfish motives. It shows that leaders should prefer persuasion over punishment.
entries.10:3: Paul admits he lives as an ordinary human being, but he insists his struggle is not fought with human weapons or tactics. Our conflicts, too, are not settled by force or scheming.
entries.10:4: The weapons Paul uses are not physical but have God's power to tear down proud human defenses. It means God's truth can break down what people build up against him.
entries.10:5: Paul's work is to demolish arguments and proud ideas that set themselves against knowing God, and to bring every thought under Christ's authority. It challenges us to let Christ rule our thinking, not just our actions.
entries.10:6: Paul is ready to discipline those who disobey once the whole church has shown it is fully obedient. It suggests that correction should come after the community has clearly committed itself to doing right.
entries.10:7: Paul tells them to look at the obvious facts: if someone claims to belong to Christ, they should recognize that Paul belongs to Christ just as much. It warns against judging others while being blind to our own claims.
entries.10:8: Paul is not ashamed to speak about the authority the Lord gave him, because that authority is meant to build people up, not tear them down. It reminds us that true authority serves others' good.
entries.10:9: Paul does not want his letters to seem like empty threats meant to frighten them. It shows he cares about being honest rather than intimidating.
entries.10:10: Some critics said Paul's letters were strong and weighty but his physical presence was weak and his speaking unimpressive. It reminds us not to judge people by appearance or speaking style.
entries.10:11: Paul says that what he writes from a distance he will also do when he arrives. It means words and actions should match, and promises should be kept.
entries.10:12: Paul refuses to compare himself with people who praise themselves, because measuring yourself by yourself is foolish. It warns against the trap of judging ourselves by our own standards.
entries.10:13: Paul will not boast beyond the limits God set for him, and those limits include the work he did among the Corinthians. It teaches us to stay within the work God actually gave us.
entries.10:14: Paul is not stretching the truth, because he really did bring the good news to them. It means we should not claim credit for things we never actually did.
entries.10:15: Paul does not want to take credit for work others did, but he hopes that as the Corinthians' faith grows, his work among them will expand. It encourages us to be glad when others' faith grows, not jealous.
entries.10:16: Paul hopes to preach the good news in lands beyond Corinth without claiming credit for work someone else had already started. It shows the value of breaking new ground rather than building on another's foundation for praise.
entries.10:17: If anyone wants to boast, they should boast about the Lord rather than about themselves. It turns our attention away from self-praise toward God.
entries.10:18: What counts is not a person's own opinion of themselves but the Lord's approval of them. It reminds us that God's judgment matters more than self-praise or others' praise.
entries.11:1: Paul asks the church to tolerate him while he says some things that sound like boasting. He knows it sounds foolish, but he wants them to hear him out because he cares about them.
entries.11:2: Paul pictures himself as a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Christ, and he wants to present the church pure and faithful to him. He is deeply concerned that they stay completely devoted to Christ.
entries.11:3: Paul worries that just as the snake tricked Eve, false teachers could trick the church into turning away from simple, sincere devotion to Christ. Readers should guard their hearts against clever deception.
entries.11:4: The church was putting up with people who preached a different Jesus, a different spirit, and a different message. Paul points out that they tolerated false teaching too easily.
entries.11:5: Paul says he is not inferior to the so-called super-apostles who were criticizing him. He refuses to accept that he is a lesser messenger.
entries.11:6: Paul admits he may not be a polished speaker, but he knows the truth deeply, and his life among them proved it. Skill in speaking is not the same as knowing the message.
entries.11:7: Paul asks if he did wrong by humbling himself and preaching God's good news to them free of charge so they could be lifted up. Serving them at his own cost was not a fault.
entries.11:8: Paul took support from other churches so he could serve the Corinthians without being a burden to them. He let others pay so this church could receive freely.
entries.11:9: When Paul was with them and needed money, he did not become a burden to anyone; friends from Macedonia supplied what he needed. He was determined to keep it that way.
entries.11:10: Paul insists, with Christ as his witness, that no one in that region will stop him from boasting about not taking their money. He is firm about this.
entries.11:11: Paul asks whether his refusal to take their money means he does not love them, and he calls God to judge his heart. His actions came from love, not rejection.
entries.11:12: Paul will keep doing what he has been doing so that the false teachers have no chance to claim they are just like him. He wants their true motives exposed.
entries.11:13: Those men are fake apostles and deceivers who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ. Not everyone who claims to represent Christ actually does.
entries.11:14: This should not surprise anyone, since even Satan can disguise himself as an angel of light. Evil often looks good and religious on the outside.
entries.11:15: So it is no surprise when Satan's servants pretend to be servants of what is right; in the end they will get what their deeds deserve. False teachers will not escape judgment.
entries.11:16: Paul asks them not to think he is foolish, but if they do, to tolerate him so he can boast a little. He is reluctantly defending himself.
entries.11:17: Paul says this boasting is not something the Lord commanded but is spoken like a foolish person taking credit for himself. He is honest that this is not his normal way.
entries.11:18: Since many others are boasting about human credentials, Paul says he will do the same. He meets them on their own ground.
entries.11:19: Paul notes, with some irony, that the wise Corinthians gladly put up with foolish people. They were tolerating the wrong people too easily.
entries.11:20: They put up with anyone who enslaved them, used them, trapped them, looked down on them, or even hit them. Paul points out how patient they were with abusive leaders.
entries.11:21: Paul says this to their shame, as if he had been too weak to act that way. But if others are bold, he says he will be bold too, even if it sounds foolish.
entries.11:22: Paul matches the false teachers point by point: if they are Hebrews, Israelites, and descendants of Abraham, so is he. He has the same heritage they boast about.
entries.11:23: Paul says he is even more a servant of Christ, though he admits it sounds like foolish boasting, and lists his harder work, more imprisonments, worse beatings, and brushes with death. His credentials are proven by suffering, not titles.
entries.11:24: Five times the Jewish authorities gave him the maximum beating of thirty-nine lashes. This shows how much hostility he faced from his own people.
entries.11:25: He was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, and shipwrecked three times, spending a night and a day adrift in the sea. His ministry cost him real physical danger.
entries.11:26: Paul faced constant dangers in travel, from rivers, robbers, his own people, foreigners, in cities, in the wilderness, at sea, and from false brothers. Danger came from every direction, including from people pretending to be friends.
entries.11:27: He worked hard and grew weary, went many nights without sleep, went hungry and thirsty, and suffered cold and lack of clothing. His service was marked by real hardship, not comfort.
entries.11:28: Beyond all that, every day he carried the weight of concern for all the churches. Leaders bear a constant burden for the people they care for.
entries.11:29: Paul feels for anyone who is weak, and he burns with concern when someone is led into sin. He does not stand apart from the struggles of others.
entries.11:30: If Paul must boast, he will boast about the things that show his weakness. He turns the world's idea of glory upside down.
entries.11:31: Paul calls on the God and Father of Jesus, who deserves praise forever, to confirm that what he says is true. He appeals to God as his witness.
entries.11:32: In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas posted guards at the city gates to arrest Paul. His enemies were powerful and determined to stop him.
entries.11:33: Paul escaped by being lowered in a basket through a window in the city wall, slipping out of their hands. God rescued him in a humble, unexpected way.
entries.12:1: Paul says that although boasting about himself is not a good thing, he will go on to describe visions and revelations God gave him. For the reader, this shows that even spiritual experiences should be shared carefully and humbly, not to impress people.
entries.12:2: Paul tells of a man he knows, a follower of Christ, who fourteen years earlier was taken up to the third heaven, though Paul doesn't know if this happened in the body or out of it. It reminds the reader that God can give real experiences beyond our understanding, and we don't need to explain everything.
entries.12:3: Paul repeats that he doesn't know whether the man was in the body or out of it, and only God knows. This honest uncertainty shows the reader that it's fine to admit what we don't know about God's workings.
entries.12:4: The man was taken into Paradise and heard words that cannot be repeated or spoken by people. This tells the reader that some things God reveals are too sacred or beyond us to put into words.
entries.12:5: Paul says he will boast about that man's experience but not about himself, except in his own weaknesses. For the reader, this means it's better to be honest about our weaknesses than to brag about our spiritual highs.
entries.12:6: Paul says that if he did boast, he would be telling the truth, not talking nonsense, but he holds back so no one thinks more of him than what they see and hear. This teaches the reader to let actions and words speak rather than self-promotion.
entries.12:7: Because the revelations were so great, Paul was given a painful thorn in the flesh, sent by Satan, to keep him from becoming proud. This shows the reader that God can use even painful struggles to keep us humble.
entries.12:8: Paul asked the Lord three times to take this thorn away. For the reader, this is an example of honest, persistent prayer when we are hurting.
entries.12:9: God's grace is enough even when you are not. His strength shows up best where you are weakest.
entries.12:10: Paul says he takes pleasure in weaknesses, insults, hardships, attacks, and troubles for Christ's sake, because when he is weak, then he is strong. This tells the reader that God's strength shows up best in our weakness.
entries.12:11: Paul says the Corinthians forced him to talk like a fool, though they should have spoken up for him; he says he is not inferior to the top apostles, even though he is nothing. This reminds the reader to support faithful leaders and to stay humble about oneself.
entries.12:12: Paul points out that the marks of a true apostle—signs, wonders, and mighty works—were done among the Corinthians with quiet strength. This tells the reader that genuine ministry is confirmed by real evidence, not just claims.
entries.12:13: Paul asks how the Corinthians were treated as less than other churches, except that he himself was never a burden to them, and he jokingly asks forgiveness for that 'wrong.' This shows the reader that a leader who gives rather than takes may be misunderstood.
entries.12:14: Paul says he is ready to come to them a third time and will not be a burden, because he wants them, not their money; parents save up for children, not the other way around. This teaches the reader that true love gives rather than uses people.
entries.12:15: Paul says he will gladly spend everything he has for their souls, and asks whether loving them more means being loved less. For the reader, this shows that genuine love keeps giving even when it isn't returned.
entries.12:16: Paul acknowledges the charge that, though he wasn't a burden himself, he might have tricked them by deceit. This shows the reader that leaders can face unfair suspicions and still respond honestly.
entries.12:17: Paul asks whether he took advantage of them through any of the men he sent. This invites the reader to check claims fairly rather than assume the worst about those who serve.
entries.12:18: Paul says he sent Titus and another brother, and asks whether Titus took advantage of them, noting that they both acted in the same Spirit and the same way. This shows the reader that consistent, honest conduct is the best answer to suspicion.
entries.12:19: Paul says it may look like they have been defending themselves all along, but they speak before God in Christ, and everything is for the Corinthians' good. This tells the reader that honest correction is meant to help, not to win an argument.
entries.12:20: Paul fears that when he comes, they may not be as he hopes and he may not be as they hope, with quarreling, jealousy, anger, divisions, gossip, pride, and disorder among them. This warns the reader that unresolved conflict and bad attitudes damage a community.
entries.12:21: Paul fears that when he returns, God may humble him before them, and he may grieve over those who sinned and never repented of their impurity and wrong desires. This reminds the reader that unrepented sin brings sorrow and that repentance matters.
entries.13:1: Paul is warning the church that this will be his third visit to them, and he will deal with problems fairly by confirming every accusation with witnesses. It means we should be fair and careful before judging anyone.
entries.13:2: Paul reminds them that he already warned the people who were sinning, and he repeats that warning now before he arrives. It means we should take warnings seriously and change our behavior before consequences come.
entries.13:3: The Corinthians wanted proof that Christ was speaking through Paul, and Paul says Christ's power was clearly at work among them. It means we shouldn't demand more proof of what God is already doing in our lives.
entries.13:4: Christ died in weakness on the cross but now lives by God's power, and Paul says he and his team share that same pattern. It means weakness and suffering don't mean God has abandoned us; his power shows up through them.
entries.13:5: Paul tells them to honestly examine themselves to see whether their faith is real and whether Christ is truly in them. It means we should regularly check our own hearts instead of only judging others.
entries.13:6: Paul hopes the Corinthians will recognize that he and his coworkers genuinely belong to Christ. It means we should give credit to those who faithfully serve God rather than doubting them.
entries.13:7: Paul prays that the Corinthians will do what is right, not so he looks good, but so they will be good. It means our goal should be doing right for its own sake, not to impress people.
entries.13:8: Paul says he and his team cannot work against the truth, only for it. It means we should always stand on the side of what is true, even when it's hard.
entries.13:9: Paul is glad to look weak if it means the Corinthians are strong and growing. It means real leaders care more about others' growth than about their own reputation.
entries.13:10: Paul writes this ahead of time so that when he comes he won't have to be harsh with them. It means honest warnings now can prevent painful correction later.
entries.13:11: Paul closes by urging them to be joyful, grow toward maturity, encourage each other, agree with one another, and live in peace. It means these simple habits invite God's love and peace into our relationships.
entries.13:12: Paul tells them to greet each other with a holy kiss, a common sign of affection and unity in that culture. It means we should warmly and sincerely welcome one another as family in Christ.
entries.13:13: Paul passes on greetings from all the believers who are with him. It means we are part of a larger family of faith and should remember and care for believers beyond our own group.
entries.13:14: Paul ends with a blessing asking for Christ's grace, God's love, and the Holy Spirit's fellowship to be with them all. It means we can rest in the grace, love, and closeness with God that he freely gives.
